transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: It is tempting to describe the invention of the printing press as a sudden revolution. Johannes Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz produced the first printed Bible in the 1450s, and within fifty years, millions of books had been printed across Europe. But historians today emphasise both the novelty of the technology and the continuity with what came before, and I want to explore that tension.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: First, what was new? Gutenberg did not invent printing. Block printing existed in China centuries earlier, and Korea had used movable metal type by the thirteenth century. His achievement was to combine several technologies: a durable alloy for casting type, an oil-based ink that adhered to metal, and a press adapted from those used for wine and olives. Importantly, the alphabet of European languages, with a few dozen characters, suited movable type far better than Chinese writing, with thousands of characters. That helps explain why the technology spread so rapidly in Europe.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: The effect on cost was dramatic. A handwritten Bible might take a scribe more than a year to copy and cost as much as a house. A printed one was a fraction of the price. By 1500, books were cheap enough for merchants, lawyers and teachers to own, not only the church and aristocracy.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Did the press cause the Reformation? Elizabeth Eisenstein argued in the 1970s that it did much to enable it. Martin Luther's pamphlets were printed in the hundreds of thousands, reaching audiences that no preacher could. But historians since have complicated this picture. Literacy was still low, perhaps ten to twenty per cent in many places, so pamphlets were often read aloud to groups. And earlier reformers, such as Jan Hus, had been silenced before the press existed. It seems fairer to say that the press amplified the Reformation rather than created it.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Another claim is that printing standardised knowledge. When texts were copied by hand, errors accumulated. Printing meant that thousands of readers saw identical text, making it possible to compare, criticise and build on one another's work. This arguably supported the growth of modern science. Yet early printed books also spread mistakes at scale, and the first printed medical textbooks contained errors that persisted for generations. Standardisation is therefore a mixed blessing.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Finally, consider the response of authority. Governments and the church recognised the power of print, and responded with licensing, censorship and lists of forbidden books. But enforcement was patchy, and printers moved to places with milder rules. In this sense, the press created a contest between control and circulation that continues today, with the internet as the latest chapter. For next week, read the extract from Eisenstein and be ready to say whether you find her argument persuasive.
